thread.title: Attorney General Nessel joins opposition to proposed Postal Service firearm mailing rule
thread.title_full: Attorney General Nessel joins opposition to proposed Postal Service firearm mailing rule

author: i. j. gardner
title: Attorney General Nessel joins opposition to proposed Postal Service firearm mailing rule
text:
Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced on May 6 that she has joined a coalition of 22 states in opposing a proposed rule by the United States Postal Service that would allow certain firearms to be mailed across state lines. The group argues that this proposal could lead to more prohibited weapons being transported through the mail, endangering public safety and increasing costs for state and local governments.
The letter from the coalition says that federal law has restricted mailing concealable firearms through the Postal Service since 1927, and asserts that only Congress—not executive agencies—can change this policy. The attorneys general warn that allowing individuals to send firearms by mail without using licensed sellers could make it easier for people who are not allowed to own guns, such as felons or domestic abusers, to obtain them. They also say it would make solving gun crimes harder and more expensive because law enforcement would lose access to key tracing tools.
“The U.S. Postal Service should not be used as a loophole for criminals to bypass Michigan law and flood our streets with untraceable firearms,” said Attorney General Nessel. “By illegally and unilaterally dismantling protections that have been in place for nearly 100 years, the Trump administration is making our communities less safe. I stand with my colleagues in opposing this absurd proposed rule.”
According to the multistate letter, if the new rule takes effect, individuals who are prohibited from owning guns—including those convicted of felonies or under restraining orders—could acquire weapons through the mail despite state laws designed to prevent this. The types of weapons sent could include those banned by some states, such as assault weapons or silencers. Unlike private carriers like UPS, USPS does not have an obligation under current statutes to ensure packages comply with individual state firearm laws.
The attorneys general also caution that without access to federal trace data on these firearms shipments, law enforcement agencies may face higher investigation costs and might need new tracking systems if unregulated firearm mailing becomes common.
Nessel was joined in signing the letter by attorneys general from Arizona, California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Hawai’i, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia Washington and the District of Columbia.

The letter from the coalition says that federal law has restricted mailing concealable firearms through the Postal Service since 1927, and asserts that only Congress—not executive agencies—can change this policy.
